findings.text: From the first paragraph alone, a newcomer can say what Athena is. It names the product, the language, what it does, and what sets it apart.
findings.source: "Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost."

findings.text: The page tells the reader what to do next. The top links straight to the next steps, and that section gives a repository link, an install command and a sample request.
findings.source: "Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself." and the Next steps section

findings.text: The install step assumes the reader already has a checkout. It gives no clone command and no prerequisites, such as a Rust toolchain or AI model access, so the reader has to go to the repository to find them.
findings.source: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh"

findings.text: Someone arriving at Athena's own site mostly reads about a different project, firstmate. After the opening paragraphs, almost nothing on the page is about Athena, how to use it, or what its output looks like for your own repository.
findings.source: Title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and sections States, Counters, Transitions, Claims and sources

findings.text: The reason the page exists is stated once, in one sentence. A newcomer has to work out for themselves that the cited claims and source links are the demonstration. The page never says why traced claims matter to someone who might use Athena.
findings.source: "Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files."

findings.text: The page defines these terms early, which helps. But the opening section packs in many specialised terms (captain, yolo, in scope, exit 75, worktree, secondmate, scout) before the reader has a reason to care. A newcomer skimming will find it hard going.

The state and transition cards give exact details, such as exit codes, guards and which claims support each step. That suits someone who wants to check how firstmate behaves, but it is far more detail than a first-time visitor needs to judge Athena.
findings.source: t2 card: "the spawn is deferred with exit 75"; Transitions cards t1–t11

findings.text: The page says plainly that the study only read firstmate's code and never ran it. That is a clear statement of its limits and helps the reader trust the claims.
findings.source: Limits of this study: "f1 ... no failure or retry edge was observed; every claim is marked read."
